extracted.intended_audience: readers of Thomas Jefferson correspondence (historians, students, general public interested in 18th-century politics and diplomacy)
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and interpret substantive evaluative principles, policy recommendations, and practical rules embedded in Thomas Jefferson's late-1780s letters (diplomatic, fiscal, constitutional, and commercial advice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue of trial / Right to be tried by law of the land
rubrics_metrics.description: If an offence is to be decided by the law of the land, the accused should be tried in the ordinary court where fellow citizens are tried (i.e., the King's Bench), not in an extraordinary court whose judges decide by discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson argues that trying a person before an extraordinary court, instead of the ordinary learned judicature, disfranchises them of the benefit of the laws and transfers them from a court of learning and integrity to one 'illiterate and unprincipled.' He cautions readers to scrutinize specious arguments in favor of extraordinary tribunals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration of rights required in new constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution should be accompanied by an explicit declaration of rights guaranteeing key civil liberties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson lists specific rights that such a declaration should stipulate: freedom of religion, freedom of the press, freedom of commerce against monopolies, trial by juries in all cases, no suspension of the habeas corpus, and no standing armies. He recommends states refuse to accede until such a declaration is annexed, as a lever to secure its adoption and to correct glaring faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to perpetual presidential re-eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Perpetual re-eligibility of the President is dangerous and should be viewed with alarm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson warns this feature will invite foreign interference (by money and even arms) to put a friend or foe in office, making the presidency of greater foreign consequence than a weak monarchy; while he recognizes difficulty of immediate amendment, he predicts long-term distress and urges care to avoid schism while seeking reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tobacco trade contract and shipping rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Tobacco contracts are forbidden until the tobacco arrives in France; tobacco must be shipped in French or American bottoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson notes the arrangement is a continuation of a five-year order (Berni) leaving price to buyer and seller but explicitly forbids pre-arrival contracts and requires use of French or American vessels—this is non-negotiable in his view and must be strictly observed by merchants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diplomatic agent selection: choose personally interested and directly involved representative
rubrics_metrics.description: When deputing an agent for settlement of claims, select someone who was directly involved in the transaction, knowledgeable, and personally interested in the outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson selects Commodore Paul Jones to carry a letter to Copenhagen and to conduct final adjustment because Jones commanded the squadron that took the prizes, can give material information, enter into conferences, and has personal and representative interest (patron of those under him), lending him adequacy and authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence of public servants in political advocacy (abolition society example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public servants should avoid overly public demonstrations on contentious causes when such publicity would impair their ability to serve or to advance the cause abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson declines formal association with a French abolition society while serving as a public official, arguing that too public a stance might reduce his capacity to help the cause internationally and that prudence demands discretion to maximize long-term effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the power to borrow as national credit tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintaining the ability to borrow is essential to national security and financial resilience, even if borrowing is generally objectionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson calls himself 'much an enemy to the system of borrowing' yet argues strongly for preserving borrowing power to avoid being overwhelmed by another nation's credit. He frames borrowing capability as strategic, not merely fiscal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loan management: timing and consolidated borrowing strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Manage foreign loans by consolidating large sums rather than making many small demands; be attentive to timing requirements and to the practicalities of producing cash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific operational notes: cash must be produced about fifteen days before it is needed (creditors require notice), executing bonds in advance can present a more favorable appearance, and asking for the whole sum at once disguises the government's feebleness better than repeated small demands. Coordinate closely with bankers to avoid signaling weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid transferring domestic debt to foreigners; keep domestic debt at home
rubrics_metrics.description: Discourage or obstruct the sale/transfer of domestic government debt to foreign holders to preserve domestic credit and borrowing capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson recommends practical measures (e.g., making the title exist in loose papers rather than only in treasury books so a foreign holder would risk title papers in America) to raise transaction costs and discourage transfers. He argues that foreign purchase of domestic debt undermines future ability to borrow abroad and damages national credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate tradeoffs of ad hoc broker/bondholder proposals carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: When brokers or holders of domestic certificates propose arrangements (e.g., taking up foreign loan remnants in exchange for retaining interest), weigh short-term relief against long-term credit consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson recounts an offer by a broker (Stanitski) to help complete a loan provided he retain one year's interest (with a 10% deduction) to be held in Europe—he advises decision-makers to judge whether such a concession (and the timing of cash delivery) is preferable to the shock to credit that might follow failure to pay interest in Amsterdam.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banking and sovereign credit practice: tie loans to taxation for reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: A nation's creditworthiness is bolstered when loans are backed by dedicated taxation and there is a consistent record of timely interest payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson cites English credit as exemplary because England 'never opens a loan without laying and appropriating taxes for the payment of the interest' and has never failed a day's payment; this is offered as a model for strengthening national credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms for foreign military service engagements
rubrics_metrics.description: Conditions for an officer entering foreign service should explicitly protect their ties to home service and limit conflicting obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regarding Commodore Paul Jones accepting a foreign (Russian) command, Jefferson notes the conditions he demanded: rank of rear-admiral, a separate command (never to be commanded), freedom at all times to return to the orders of Congress, and not being expected to bear arms against France. These condition-types are recommended as safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize infrastructure projects by strategic commercial impact (Potomac canal example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select public works that will capture and direct major future commercial flows; such projects should be considered of highest priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson identifies opening a canal between the Cayahoga and Big Beaver as 'the most important work' Virginia could undertake because it would direct commerce from Lake Erie through the Potomac, shaping regional trade routes. He recommends studying existing examples (e.g., canal of Languedoc) and adapting lessons.
